https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.question: Can a cultural tradition count as a living system?
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.thesis: Jonathan Loh proposes that culturally transmitted information is a genuine evolving form of life, rather than merely a metaphor.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.argument: Traditions are copied, varied, selected and transmitted between individuals. Language improves the fidelity and complexity of this process. Loh argues that replication and evolution of information can define life beyond DNA-based organisms.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.intellectual_background: The argument draws on cultural evolution, social learning, and debates about the definition of life; it extends but is not equivalent to biological evolution.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.example: A song learned by successive generations persists and changes even as every individual performer eventually dies.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.strongest_objection: Replication and adaptation alone may not suffice for life: computer files and contagious rumors also propagate, but they lack autonomous metabolism or biological organization.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.possible_response: Loh's broader informational definition deliberately challenges cell-centered criteria, though it needs clear boundaries to avoid treating every copied pattern as alive.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.implications: The view changes how we describe culture, education and artificial systems without proving that AI systems are organisms.
